name: United Arab Emirates
summary: Seven emirates (the former Trucial States) that united in 1971; oil wealth turned Dubai and Abu Dhabi into global cities.

knownFor.label: Dubai airport
knownFor.note: One of the busiest for international travel.

location.value: West Asia, at the eastern end of the Arabian Peninsula.

terrain.value: Mostly desert, with a coastal plain and the Hajar Mountains.

climate.value: Desert climate: hot summers (above 45 °C on the coast in July and August) and warm winters.

resources.value: The world’s seventh-largest oil reserves and seventh-largest natural gas reserves.

disasters.value: Record floods hit the emirates in April 2024.

population.value: Over 11 million; only about 11% are native Emiratis.

urbanisation.value: Dubai is the largest city; Abu Dhabi is the capital.

disease.value: Ranks highly for healthcare and other social indicators.

migration.value: Most residents are expatriates and migrant workers, mainly from South Asia.

economicBase.value: Oil and gas (26% of GDP in 2018), plus tourism, finance and business.

tradeRoutes.value: Ports such as Jebel Ali and Khalifa; Dubai International Airport, the world’s busiest for international passengers.

wealth.value: A high-income economy built on oil, trade, finance and tourism.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: A federal semi-constitutional monarchy of seven emirates.

keyRulers.value: Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan (first president, 1971–2004). Later and present leaders are not named here.

succession.value: The Federal Supreme Council of the seven rulers elects the president and vice president.

institutions.value: The Federal Supreme Council of the seven rulers, the highest authority, and the advisory Federal National Council.

stability.value: Politically stable, with power held by the ruling families of the emirates.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: Armed forces deployed abroad, including in Somalia, Kosovo, Afghanistan, Libya and Yemen.

majorWars.value: Troops fought in Yemen; 52 soldiers were killed in the 2015 Marib attack.

territoryChange.value: Since 1971 the UAE has disputed three Gulf islands held by Iran: Abu Musa, Greater Tunb and Lesser Tunb.

alliancesRivals.value: Founding member of the Gulf Cooperation Council (1981); Abraham Accords with Israel (2020).

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: The Hope probe reached Mars orbit in 2021, the first Arab mission to Mars.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: The Dubai Metro, the first urban train network in the Arabian Peninsula; major international airports.

religion.value: Islam is the state religion; there is a Christian minority among the many migrants.

languageWriting.value: Arabic is official; English is the most spoken language and the language of business.

artsArchitecture.value: Grand cultural projects in Abu Dhabi include the Louvre Abu Dhabi and the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi.

socialStructure.value: Native Emiratis are only about 11% of the population; most residents are expatriates.

sharedIdentity.value: An Emirati identity based on Gulf Arab heritage, though most residents are foreign workers.

dailyLife.value: Dishes include machboos, threed and khameer bread; lugaimat is a famous dessert.

neighbours.value: Oman and Saudi Arabia by land; sea borders with Qatar and Iran.

ideasReligions.value: A global trade hub, with Islam the state religion and many other communities present.

colonisation.value: Britain signed a maritime truce with local rulers in 1820, creating the Trucial States, a British protectorate from 1892 until independence in 1971.

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: The United Arab Emirates continue as a federation.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
